sens: Moving air
Storm, gust
Figuratively: destructive or divine power
H6500.detail: 1. The wind is a moving breath of air, a natural force that is unseen but whose effects are felt (Hosea 13:15: "the east wind will come"). 2. In particular, the wind can be violent and destructive, like a storm that dries up and devastates (Hosea 13:15: "He will dry up its springs, and will make its fountains dry"). 3. Figuratively, the wind represents the action of God, His power that blows where it wills and can both give life or judge: it is "the wind of the Lord" that rises from the desert to chastise.
H6500.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that designates breath, moving air. It is a variant of pāra (H6509) and is rooted in the primary image of the divine breath that animates creation — the same word is linked to the verb "to breathe" and the idea of vital force.
H6500.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Hosea 13:15. In this passage, the prophet Hosea describes God's judgment on Ephraim (the northern kingdom): despite its apparent fertility, the desert wind — a symbol of divine anger — will come to dry it up. The image of the devastating wind is very frequent in the Bible to express God's judgment or destructive power.
H6500.portee: This verse reminds us that human prosperity, even when it seems assured, remains fragile before God. The wind of divine judgment blows where it wills and overturns the certainties of nations that forget the Lord. It is a call not to trust in wealth or strength, but to fear and serve the living God.

sens: Wild equid of the desert, untamed and independent animal
Vagabond animal that seeks its food alone in arid lands
Free creature, unbound, symbol of independence and solitude
Figuratively: man or people characterized by insubordination or wandering
H6501.detail:
1. The wild donkey is an equid that lives freely in the deserts and arid regions of the Near East, very different from the domestic donkey. It is a robust and independent animal, impossible to tame, that recognizes no master. Job 39:8 celebrates it: "Who sets the wild donkey free, and who loosens the bonds of the wild donkey?" — the very image of fierce freedom.
2. This vagabond animal roams the desert in search of food, without a fixed dwelling, without security. Job 24:5 describes it going out in the morning to seek food for itself and its young: it symbolizes the precarious and solitary life of the poor or the refugee.
3. In the prophetic vision, the wild donkey becomes a sign of desolation: the ruins where it brays (Isaiah 32:14, Jeremiah 14:6) evoke a territory empty, left to itself, once fertile but now become a desert.
4. Figuratively, Scripture compares a fiery and rebellious man to this animal: Genesis 16:12 predicts of Ishmael that "he will be like a wild donkey," meaning a character that is free, violent, and an enemy to all — an image of a life marked by conflict and isolation.
H6501.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּרֶא (péré) specifically designates the wild donkey, distinct from the domestic donkey (חָמוֹר, chamôr). Its etymology refers to the idea of fierce freedom and independence. This word appears mainly in biblical poetry and wisdom texts, where it serves to evoke the untamed and free nature of creation, or to characterize by contrast the rebellious man.
H6501.emploi: The word appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetic contexts: in Job (five times), where it illustrates the divine wisdom that maintains wild creatures in their natural freedom, and in the Psalms and prophets (five times), where it symbolizes either desolation or revolt. In Genesis 16:12, it predicts Ishmael's turbulent character. In Jeremiah 2:24, the people of Israel is compared to a wild donkey in heat, an image of unfaithfulness and uncontrollability. In the wisdom texts (Job), the wild donkey becomes a wonder of creation, proof that God provides for all living beings, even the most free and distant from man.
H6501.portee: The wild donkey reminds us that God is the creator and protector of all living creatures, including those who refuse the human yoke — a lesson in humility in the face of the limits of our power. As a figure of man, it embodies the danger of carnal independence: one who refuses to follow God's will becomes like a wild beast, incapable of peace or alliance. For the believer, this word invites us to seek not the false freedom of rebellion, but the true freedom of obedience.

sens: Amorite king of Jarmuth at the time of Israel's conquest
H6502.detail: Pirham is an Amorite king who ruled the city of Jarmuth during the invasion of Canaan by Joshua. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, during the coalition of five Amorite kings against Israel (Joshua 10:3). His name literally means "like a wild donkey," which evokes strength and pride. Pirham was among the local rulers of Canaan whom Joshua defeated, but he is not described individually: only his title and political role matter for the biblical narrative.
H6502.origine: The name Pirham means "like a wild donkey" in ancient Hebrew. This image evokes the brute strength and fierce independence of the wild beast. It is a typical nickname for Amorite kings, revealing how they were viewed: as impetuous and untamed warriors, embodying power but also the absence of divine wisdom.
H6502.emploi: Pirham appears only once in the entire Bible, in Joshua 10:3. He is cited as one of the five Amorite kings who, under the leadership of Adoni-Zedek, king of Jerusalem, conspired against Joshua and Israel. Although his name is mentioned alongside those of the other defeated kings, the Bible reports no specific details about his life, actions, or death. His appearance is purely enumerative: he represents the organized Canaanite resistance against the Israelite conquest.

sens: annex building of Solomon's temple
open structure adjacent to the temple
H6503.detail: Parbar is a construction attached to Solomon's temple, probably on its west side. The word designates an open structure, perhaps a gallery or portico. It is mentioned in the context of the religious reforms of King Josiah, who ordered the destruction of the idols there (2 Kings 23:11), and in the account of the duties of the temple gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 26:18). It is a building belonging to the entire sanctuary, intended for certain liturgical or administrative uses.
H6503.origine: The Hebrew word פַּרְוָר (parbar) has uncertain etymology, possibly borrowed from a neighboring language. It specifically designates this structure of Solomon's temple. No other certain occurrence of this word appears in the Bible.
H6503.emploi: Parbar appears only twice in the Bible. The first mention is in 2 Kings 23:11, at the time when King Josiah, reforming worship, orders the destruction of the horses dedicated to the sun that were there. The second mention, in 1 Chronicles 26:18, situates a gate of the Parbar among the temple guard posts, under the responsibility of the Levites. These two occurrences suggest that Parbar was a known place of the temple, serving as a depot or monitored passage.
H6503.portee: This word reminds us that Solomon's temple was a complex structure, with dependencies and annexes, not just the sanctuary itself. It also testifies to the vigilance of religious reformers who, like Josiah, sought to eliminate idolatrous practices even in the corners of the temple.

sens: Divide into two or more parts
Detach from a person or group
Move away in space
Disperse, spread out in different places
Break a bond or relationship
Be kept apart, isolated
H6504.detail:
1. Divide a whole into distinct parts: the word describes the action of splitting something that is whole into several portions. Genesis 2:10 speaks of a river that "divided into four branches."
2. Detach or separate from a person: this means leaving someone, breaking proximity. Abram and Lot "separate" from each other in Genesis 13:11 and 13:14 to live on different lands.
3. Physically move away: put distance between oneself and others. Heber the Kenite "had separated" from his people in Judges 4:11.
4. Spread out, disseminate over an area: the word denotes a dispersion without a definitive break. In Nehemiah 4:19, the builders are "dispersed" on the wall, each at their post.
5. Break or weaken a bond, a friendship: figuratively, separation can mean the loss of a deep union. Psalms 22:15 describes the psalmist whose bones "separate," an image of physical decomposition and destitution.
6. Be kept apart, live isolated: Proverbs 18:1 speaks of one who "isolates himself" and seeks only his own pleasure.
H6504.origine: The Hebrew root פרד (p-r-d) evokes the fundamental idea of splitting and breaking. It appears in several grammatical forms (simple, passive, causative, reflexive) to express the act of separating or the state of being separated. The corresponding Hebrew word in Aramaic bédhar (בְּדַר) means "to disperse" and shares the same semantic family. This root belongs to the concrete vocabulary of the ancient world: it applies to the division of territory, the separation of people, and the dispersion of a group.
H6504.emploi: The verb "separate" appears 26 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives and Proverbs. In Genesis, it expresses the division of continents (Genesis 10:5, 10:32) and the separation of patriarchs (Genesis 13, 25:23). In Psalms and Job, it takes on a poetic and often dramatic turn: bones that separate, limbs that dislocate, the image of a body that disintegrates (Psalms 22:15). Proverbs uses it to speak of voluntary or involuntary solitude, the breaking of friendship (Proverbs 16:28, 17:9, 19:4), showing how choices and conflicts fragment human bonds. In Nehemiah and Esther, the word also describes the geographical dispersion of a people or group.
H6504.portee: This word reminds us that separation marks the human condition: it can be physical, relational, or spiritual. It can be voluntary (choosing to withdraw) or imposed (being dispersed, fragmented). For the believer, understanding this notion invites reflection on the causes of rupture — pride, selfishness (Proverbs 18:1), jealousy (Proverbs 16:28) — and on the importance of preserving unity with others. It also highlights the fragility of the body and soul in the face of trials, an image that the Psalms use to express distress before God.

sens: Pack and riding animal, hybrid of horse and donkey
Beast of burden used for transporting loads
Prestigious mount in royal processions and caravans
Robust and enduring animal, compared to stupidity
H6505.detail:
1. The mule is the hybrid animal born of a horse and a donkey. It is a robust pack and riding animal, widely used in the ancient Near East. Amnon "mounted his mule" to flee after his death (2 Samuel 13:29): the mule was a reliable means of transport for travel.
2. The mule is used to carry loads: Naaman requests "a load of two mules" of earth (2 Kings 5:17), to physically carry the material he brings home. It is a pack animal used in caravans.
3. The mule figures in royal processions and solemn offerings: visitors to Solomon bring "horses and mules" each year (1 Kings 10:25), a sign of wealth and honor. Isaiah prophesies that the nations will bring the captive Israelites "on horses, chariots, and litters, on mules and camels" to Jerusalem (Isaiah 66:20).
4. The mule is mentioned in Psalm 32:9 for its lack of intelligence: "Do not be like the horse or the mule, which have no understanding" — the animal obeys by bit and bridle, not by reason.
H6505.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּרֶד (péred) specifically refers to the mule. It is also found in Akkadian and Aramaic in similar forms. The mule, whether a natural or intentionally produced hybrid, was known throughout the ancient Near East for its robustness and endurance — qualities of the horse combined with the resilience of the donkey. The Bible mentions it mainly in contexts of wealth, transport, or royal caravans.
H6505.emploi: The word "mule" appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah). It always refers to a real animal, never figuratively except in Psalm 32:9. Mules appear in three contexts: urgent or elegant travel (Amnon's flight, Absalom riding his mule), royal treasures (gifts at the courts of kings), and solemn processions or lists of possessions (the number of mules counted among the goods returned from exile). The word is purely descriptive and concrete, without major symbolic charge.
H6505.portee: The mule reminds us that the Bible speaks of a concrete world, with its animals and means of transport. It also symbolizes, in Psalm 32:9, the difference between foolish obedience (that of the beast that acts only under constraint) and intelligent obedience of the child of God, who understands and loves the will of his Father. It is an invitation not to act blindly, but with discernment and heart.

sens: Hybrid animal, robust and reliable mount
Symbol of royalty and authority
H6506.detail:
1. The mule is an animal resulting from the crossbreeding of a donkey and a mare. Robust, resilient, and reliable, it was prized as a prestigious mount in the ancient East, especially for members of the royal family and high dignitaries. In the account of Solomon's anointing, the young prince is mounted on "the mule of King David" (1 Kings 1:38), a solemn act that publicly manifests his legitimacy and choice as heir to the throne.
2. Riding a royal mule was an honor, a visible sign of power and royal favor. This usage persists in the Scriptures as a social marker: only kings and their close dignitaries rode these precious animals, while ordinary people used donkeys or horses. This is why King David expressly entrusts his own mule for this anointing ceremony.
H6506.origine: The Hebrew word pirdah specifically refers to the female hybrid (the female mule). It is related to terms designating mules and muleteers. The Hebrews borrowed this word from neighboring cultures of the Levant, where breeding these hybrids was common. The animal itself, a product of voluntary crossbreeding between two species, represented a skill and wealth that only royal courts could afford.
H6506.emploi: The word mule (pirdah) appears three times in the Bible, all in the context of Solomon's accession to the throne (1 Kings 1:33, 1:38, 1:44). Each mention reinforces the symbolic weight of this animal in the scene: first, King David orders his servants to have his son Solomon ride on his own mule to lead him to Gihon, where he will be anointed king; then, the royal officials carry out this order by bringing the young prince on "the mule of King David"; finally, the news is reported to King Adonijah as proof of Solomon's royal anointing. The animal thus becomes a silent but indispensable witness to the transmission of power.
H6506.portee: This account teaches that the legitimate succession to the throne of Israel is not arbitrary, but solemn and public. The use of the royal mule symbolizes that power comes from God through the reigning king, and that anointing (the action of the Holy Spirit) confers visible and recognized authority. For the believer, this reminds us that all true power bears the mark of God and is exercised with wisdom and dignity, not by brute force.

sens: Grain intended to be sown
Wheat or other grain stored for sowing
Figuratively, offspring or descendants
H6507.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the seed that is sown in the ground to yield a harvest: it is the grain of wheat, barley, or another plant, as it is entrusted to the soil. In Joel 1:17, the seeds have dried up under the clods of earth, a sign of the catastrophe sent by God — there will be no new harvest.
2. More broadly, this word refers to the grain stored in granaries for future sowing: it is the seed as a resource, a reserve of life for the coming season. When the granaries are empty and the seeds are dried up, it announces famine and judgment.
3. In a figurative sense, seed can represent descendants or posterity: those who are born of someone are their seeds, like the grain that grows from the sown seed.
H6507.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root (פרד) that evokes the idea of separating or dividing. The seed is this particular, distinct, and separated grain, intended to be sown alone and to produce a harvest. This image of the individual grain that carries within it the promise of an abundant harvest runs throughout biblical thought.
H6507.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Joel 1:17. The prophet Joel describes the disaster caused by the locusts: the seeds dry up, the granaries empty, all hope of harvest disappears. It is a moment of judgment where God deprives His people of the means to live. The unique use of this term reinforces its dramatic weight: it is the very word of agricultural ruin.
H6507.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the seed is both a fragile reality and a sign of hope. It depends entirely on God — on the soil, the rain, His blessings. When the seeds are lacking, it is because God has withdrawn His hand. But the seed also speaks of promise: the one who sows hopes for a harvest. This invites the reader to trust God even in times of scarcity, and to understand that divine judgment can suspend His material blessings.

sens: Cultivated space planted with trees and plants
Orchard or park arranged by a king or a wealthy man
Place of abundance and beauty, an image of delights
H6508.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a closed and cultivated space, planted with fruit trees and vegetation: it is a garden or an orchard, like the one that the wise man in Ecclesiastes had planted with "fruit trees of all kinds" (Ecclesiastes 2:5). 2. It can also refer to a garden or park arranged by a great person, a king, for his pleasure or resources: the context of Nehemiah speaks of Asaph, "the king's forest keeper," responsible for providing wood (Nehemiah 2:8). 3. Figuratively, the word evokes beauty, richness, and delights: the "garden" of the Song of Solomon (4:13) is an image of lushness, planted with pomegranates and fragrant plants, a symbol of seduction and abundance.
H6508.origine: The word comes from a root that expresses the idea of a closed and arranged space. It may have an ancient Iranian origin, also attested in Persian, reflecting the prestigious gardens of Eastern kings, places of greenery and refinement in arid regions. The word passes into ancient Greek ("paradeisos"), then into Latin and modern languages: it is recognized in our word "paradise."
H6508.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Nehemiah (2:8), it refers to the royal forest domain from which the construction wood comes. In Ecclesiastes (2:5), it refers to the gardens and orchards that the wise man appropriates to taste all pleasures. In the Song (4:13), it becomes an image of beauty and seduction, a lush refuge. Each time, the word refers to a space of wealth and mastery, sometimes useful, sometimes aesthetic, always marked by abundance and arrangement.
H6508.portee: This word reminds us that God loves created beauty and well-ordered things. It invites us to see in a garden not only a place of food but also of joy, relaxation, and contemplation. The mention of the king's garden in Nehemiah also emphasizes that the resources of the earth are given for both utility and enjoyment, and that they can be received with gratitude from God.

sens: To produce many fruits or seeds
To multiply, increase in number (for living beings)
To prosper, grow abundantly
To give birth to a numerous offspring
To spread, develop (for a plant or branch)
H6509.detail:
1. The primary sense is literal: to produce many fruits, like a fruitful tree or plant. Isaiah 11:1 speaks of a "shoot" that will come forth from the roots of Jesse, the image of a fertile branch springing from the trunk.
2. When speaking of living beings, the verb means to multiply, to increase rapidly in number. Genesis 1:22 shows God blessing the animals by saying, "Be fruitful, multiply," a command understood by both fish and birds.
3. For man and peoples, to be fruitful means to have a numerous offspring and to prosper. Genesis 28:3 expresses this blessing: "May God Almighty make you fruitful and multiply you, that you may become a multitude of peoples."
4. The verb is also used in the Hiphil (causative form) to mean "to make fruitful," "to fertilize," a divine action of blessing: Leviticus 26:9 promises, "I will make you fruitful and multiply you."
5. For plants, the word describes lush growth and expansion: Ezekiel 19:10 describes a "fruitful" vine that spreads everywhere, an image of prosperity and strength.
H6509.origine: The root פרה (parah) primarily evokes the idea of fructification and profusion. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words designating productivity and abundance. The verb appears from the very first creation narratives of the Bible, where God blesses the creatures by calling them to be fruitful. Its use in the Old Testament always links this notion to divine blessing and the fulfillment of God's plan.
H6509.emploi: This verb appears 28 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in Genesis (11 occurrences) and scattered throughout the legislative and prophetic books. Genesis uses it to express the fundamental blessing of the Creator: as early as 1:22, He commands the animals to be fruitful; in 1:28 and 9:1, He blesses humanity with the same command. This blessing personalizes in the promises made to the patriarchs: God will make Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob "fruitful," and from their lineages will come peoples (17:6, 26:22, 28:3, 35:11). Exodus 1:7 shows how Israel in Egypt multiplies prodigiously, a fruit of this blessing. The prophets use it to announce the restoration of Israel: Jeremiah 23:3 promises that God will gather the remnant who will "be fruitful." Isaiah 11:1 transposes the image to a messianic shoot. The word remains always linked to providence and divine action of blessing.
H6509.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that divine blessing is primarily expressed through fruitfulness and multiplication. It concerns not only biological offspring but also spiritual growth, the expansion of God's kingdom, and the fulfillment of His promises. In Genesis, it is the first command given to humanity: to be fruitful is a call to participate in God's creative work and to fill the earth. This promise, renewed to the patriarchs, assures the believer that God blesses life and generates it abundantly, even in times of apparent barrenness.

sens: Female bovine, livestock animal
Heifer, young cow
Ritual animal for sacrifices or purification rites
Image of prosperity or abundance
Image of fatness and well-being
Image of rebellion or hardness
H6510.detail:
1. The cow is a common livestock animal in the ancient Near East, raised for its milk, meat, and labor. In Genesis 32:15, Jacob offers cows from his herd to Esau.
2. A heifer is a young cow, often of breeding age. The text distinguishes between "cows" and "heifers" based on the age and vigor of the animal.
3. The red heifer in Numbers 19:2 is central to a unique purification rite in Israel: completely burned, its ashes mixed with water form the purifying water to cleanse one who has touched a dead body.
4. In Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41:4, 20), seven fat and beautiful cows symbolize years of abundance, while the thin and ugly cows represent famine: it is the very image of wealth that disappears.
5. "Cows" here signifies a fullness, a prosperous fatness — what Egypt possessed and risked losing.
6. In Amos 4:1, the "cows of Bashan" — fat and well-fed — describe the wealthy women of Israel who oppress the poor, durable and carefree like beasts.
H6510.origine: The Hebrew word פָּרָה comes from a root that evokes fertility and multiplication. Indeed, the cow was a symbol of generative life in many ancient cultures. In the Greek Septuagint, this word is translated as "bovis" or "damalis" (heifer). The word belongs to the family of terms designating cattle, such as "par" (bull) and "parim" (bulls).
H6510.emploi: The word appears 22 times in the Bible, mainly in Genesis (the dream of the Egyptian cows to Pharaoh), in Numbers (the rite of the red heifer, a key passage for the study of the Israelite sacrificial system), and in historical and prophetic narratives. In Genesis 41, the cow is the very language of the dream: it carries a symbolic meaning, animal and easily recognizable for an Egyptian. In Numbers 19, the cow becomes a cultic object, pure and without defect. In the prophets (Amos 4:1, Hosea 4:16, Isaiah 11:7), the cow takes on figurative meanings: wealth, rebellion, or, on the contrary, a messianic image of peace where the wolf and the heifer will graze together.
H6510.portee: The account of Pharaoh's dream teaches how God communicates His will through images that everyone understands, and how interpretation reveals His hidden plan. The rite of the red heifer reveals a God who organizes purity and holiness even in material details: no act escapes His holiness. For the prophet Amos, the cow invites reflection: wealth and comfort must never stifle justice or mercy.

sens: City of the tribe of Benjamin
H6511.detail: Para is a small town located in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible during the enumeration of localities in this region (Joshua 18:23).
H6511.origine: The name Para comes from a Hebrew root meaning "heifer" or "young female cow"; the name may suggest a connection with livestock raising or the fertility of the soil in this region.
H6511.emploi: Para appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 18:23, during the division of the lands among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. It is listed among the cities assigned to Benjamin, between Avvim and Ophra, indicating its location in this area.

sens: Small burrowing animal that lives underground
Creature considered unclean in the Law of Moses
H6512.detail:
1. The mole is an animal that digs into the soil and lives in underground tunnels. In Isaiah 2:20, it is mentioned alongside the bat, two creatures that inhabit dark and underground areas, often associated with darkness and ritual impurity.
2. According to the Law given to Moses, this animal was classified among the unclean creatures that the Israelites were not to eat or touch. By mentioning moles in Isaiah 2:20, the prophet emphasizes the contrast between the precious gold and silver of idols and the underground and filthy beasts: people will flee from their idols to throw them to the most despised creatures.
H6512.origine: The Hebrew word פְּרָה (pérah) specifically designates this burrowing animal. Its etymology suggests the idea of digging or burrowing. In Hebrew, the same lexical field includes the names of other underground or unclean animals, confirming that this word refers to a creature linked to the earth and underground regions.
H6512.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 2:20. The prophet denounces idolatry: on the day of judgment, men will reject their precious idols and throw them to moles and bats, impure and underground creatures. This image underscores the despicable and vain nature of idolatry: false deities are no better than food for filthy beasts.
H6512.portee: This word reminds us that everything that diverts us from God, even if it is precious in the eyes of the world, will ultimately be cast away as worthless. Isaiah invites the reader not to place their trust in riches or human creations, for they hold no weight before the Lord.

sens: servant of Gideon
warrior assisting the leader
confidant of Gideon
H6513.detail: 1. Pura is the servant of Gideon, mentioned twice in the account of Judges 7. He is probably Gideon's squire, accompanying him into battle and assisting him. 2. He plays a role of moral and practical support: when Gideon fears to go down to the camp of the Midianites, Pura accompanies him, which strengthens him and enables him to act (Judges 7:10-11). 3. His name means "branch" or "twig," perhaps evoking the flexibility and adaptability of the warrior who follows his leader.
H6513.origine: The name Pura comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the branch or twig of a tree. This type of animal or plant name was common in Israel to denote qualities or circumstances of birth. Pura belongs to the generation of warriors during the time of the Judges, before the monarchy in Israel.
H6513.emploi: Pura appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the same passage (Judges 7:10-11). He is presented as Gideon's faithful servant during the night when Gideon spies on the enemy camp. His presence reassures Gideon and prepares him for action. Although not detailed, his role illustrates the importance of a trusted companion in times of doubt and decision.
H6513.portee: The figure of Pura reminds us that humble and faithful servants play an essential role in God's great acts. Pura is not the hero, but his presence alongside Gideon strengthens the heart of the leader and allows God to act. This invites the reader to see the value of discreet loyalty and fraternal support in faith.

sens: Ancestor of a family of temple servants returned from exile
H6514.detail: Peruda is the name of a man living during the Babylonian exile and the return to Judea. He appears in the lists of descendants of Solomon's servants who returned to the promised land with Zerubbabel after the captivity. His name also designates the entire family that is descended from him.
H6514.origine: The name Peruda literally means "grain" or "kernel" in Hebrew. It is a name that perhaps emphasizes the idea of something vital and essential — the grain that contains life and fertility. Although rare, this name fits within a Hebrew tradition of giving names evocative of concrete and fruitful realities.
H6514.emploi: Peruda appears only twice in the Bible. The first occurrence is in Ezra 2:55, where he is mentioned as the ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from exile with Zerubbabel. The second occurrence, in Nehemiah 7:57, provides the same information in a parallel list, but the name is spelled slightly differently (Perida). This orthographic variation is common in ancient genealogical lists in the Bible. These two passages attest that a branch of temple servants bore the name Peruda and that it survived the Babylonian exile.

sens: Father of Josaphat, supply officer of King Solomon
H6515.detail: Paruach is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the enumeration of the twelve officers that King Solomon established to administer his kingdom and provide for its needs. He is known only as the father of Josaphat, who was in charge of supplying food for the region of Issachar (1 Kings 4:17). His name remains in the royal genealogies of Israel, testifying to the administrative organization of the unified kingdom under Solomon.
H6515.origine: The name Paruach literally means "sprout" or "bud" — an image of youth or growth. It is a Hebrew name formed from the root that evokes what grows, what unfolds. Although Paruach himself is known to us only through this brief mention, his son Josaphat played a visible role in Solomon's government.
H6515.emploi: Paruach appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Kings 4:17, in the official list of the twelve commissioners that Solomon appointed to administer the twelve districts of Israel and ensure his supply. He is identified there solely by his paternity: he is the father of Josaphat, the officer of Issachar. This administrative context shows that, even though Paruach left only a minor trace in biblical history, he belonged to the ruling elite of the kingdom of Israel at the time of its glory.

sens: eastern region renowned for its gold production
H6516.detail: Parvaïm is a distant region, located to the east, known in antiquity for its gold mines or exceptional gold wealth. Although its exact location remains debated among historians, the biblical text mentions it to highlight the prestigious origin of the gold used in the temple: it is with gold from Parvaïm that King Solomon adorned the house of God (2 Chronicles 3:6).
H6516.origine: The name Parvaïm literally means "eastern regions" in Hebrew. It likely designates a distant region of Arabia or the southeast, renowned for its wealth. The word evokes exoticism and opulence — what comes from so far can only be precious and rare.
H6516.emploi: Parvaïm appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 3:6, during the description of the ornamentation of the temple of Jerusalem built by Solomon. The context shows that the kings of Israel sought gold from Parvaïm particularly for sacred works, as this metal was reputed to be superior and worthy of honoring God.
H6516.portee: Parvaïm illustrates the magnificence and wealth of the temple of Jerusalem, the ultimate goal of King Solomon's devotion. By specifically mentioning this distant region, the text emphasizes that only the best — what comes from farther away, what is rarer — was deemed worthy of the house of God. It is an invitation to give to God not the ordinary, but what we have that is most precious.

sens: Container made of clay or metal used for cooking
Kitchenware used to prepare or serve food
Container in which liquids are stored or transported
H6517.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to a cooking pot, that is, a container in which food is prepared over fire. In Numbers 11:8, the manna was cooked in the pot, transformed into cakes with oil: it is the vessel where food is mixed and heated. 2. It is also an ordinary kitchen utensil among others. In 1 Samuel 2:14, the pot is mentioned alongside the cauldron, the kettle, and the stew pot: similar containers, varied in size or shape, in which the meat of the sacrifices is cooked. 3. The pot can hold and transport liquids. In Judges 6:19, Gideon puts the broth in a pot to bring it to the angel of the Lord: it is a simple and practical container for pouring or storing.
H6517.origine: The Hebrew word parur comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging or forming a hollow object. It is a simple and concrete word, one that an Israelite child would learn by watching his mother prepare a meal. The pot was a common utensil, shaped from clay, fundamental to daily life.
H6517.emploi: The word appears three times in the Old Testament, always to designate a kitchen utensil intended for cooking. It appears mainly in the context of meals or sacrifices: the preparation of the manna (Numbers 11), the meal offered to the angel (Judges 6), the handling of sacrificial meats (1 Samuel 2). In each case, the pot is a human, ordinary object, without symbolic dimension: it simply serves to transform raw food into cooked and consumable food.
H6517.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of ordinary life in the biblical narrative. The Bible does not disdain concrete details: it is interested in meals, cooking, utensils. By mentioning the pot, it affirms that even the simplest acts of feeding one's people or guests are worthy of being told. Daily life, the shared table, is the place where God acts and reveals Himself.

sens: Military leader, warrior who commands
Person of power or authority
H6518.detail:
1. Military leader, warrior who commands: the word evokes a leader of a band or a warrior who leads his men into battle. In Habakkuk 3:14, the prophet speaks of the "leaders" of the enemies whom God pierces with His arrows, the front-line fighters who rush against the people of God.
2. Person of power or authority: the term can more broadly refer to one who exercises power, who directs a group. The military context dominates here in the unique biblical occurrence.
H6518.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּרֶז (pérez) is difficult to explain with certainty; its root may be related to the idea of breaking or strength. It appears only once in the Bible in Hebrew, making its interpretation challenging. Ancient Greek translators and early versions inferred its meaning from the context: warriors or enemy leaders who attack violently.
H6518.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Habakkuk 3:14. In this passage of the prophetic song, it refers to the leaders or warriors of the enemy peoples who rush against the people of God to destroy them. God pierces them with His arrows — it is an image of His victory and protection over His people. The unique and martial use of the term makes it a specialized word to describe the adversaries of God's people.
H6518.portee: This passage reminds us that even the most powerful leaders and the most fearsome warriors can do nothing against the people of God when they remain under His protection. The prophetic vision shows us that our trust should not rest on human strength, but on the power of the God who defends His own.

sens: Rural locality without fortifications
Open and vulnerable region
Dispersed and undefended habitat
H6519.detail: 1. This word refers to a small human settlement, a hamlet or village lacking walls and fortified gates. In Esther 9:19, the Jews who live in "unwalled towns" are clearly inhabitants of unprotected rural areas, unlike the large cities. 2. The absence of walls characterizes an open territory vulnerable to attacks. Ezekiel 38:11 describes an invasion of a "land of unwalled villages" where people live "safely," but precisely because they do not suspect the impending danger — indicating that these places are not fortified. 3. By extension, the word evokes a dispersed habitat, without organized defensive structures. Zechariah 2:4 proclaims that Jerusalem will be "an open city," meaning it will no longer need walls: its abundance of inhabitants and livestock will be its natural protection.
H6519.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes what is "open," "bare," "unprotected." It stands in contrast to a fortified city with walls and gates. In biblical Hebrew, the state of "open village" reflects the geographical and social situation of small rural communities that, unlike large royal cities, lacked architectural defenses.
H6519.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Esther 9:19, it describes the rural Jewish dwellings during the Feast of Purim. In Ezekiel 38:11, it characterizes the lands of Israel as vulnerable to the invasion of Gog — an "open" and unsuspecting land. In Zechariah 2:4, it expresses a messianic promise: Jerusalem will become so prosperous and populated that it will not need walls for protection. In each case, the word emphasizes the absence of fortifications, but with different implications: practical vulnerability, or — in Zechariah — a promise of security through abundance.
H6519.portee: This word reminds us that the true security of God's people does not rest on walls or human defenses, but on divine protection. Zechariah 2:4 announces a transformation where the absence of walls becomes a sign of blessing and trust, not weakness: God Himself becomes the guard of His people.

sens: person who leads a rural community or an unwalled town
local authority exercising command and responsibility over the people
H6520.detail:
1. The word originally designates a person of responsibility in rural areas or unwalled villages — places less significant and less protected than large fortified cities. In Judges 5:7, it is said that "the leaders were lacking in Israel": these local authorities are absent, leaving the people without direction.
2. More broadly, this term evokes the role of guide and protector of a community. The Song of Deborah (Judges 5:11) celebrates "the blessings of her leader in Israel" — the poetic expression of one who leads his people to deliverance and victory, the one in whom divine leadership and authority rest.
H6520.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning probably "to spread" or "to be open" (open village, without rampart), hence the idea of a rural community. The form is a collective or singular noun designating the role of one who presides over such a community. Its exact etymology remains debated among Hebrew scholars, but the biblical context clearly shows that it is a function of chief or leader.
H6520.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Judges 5, the Song of Deborah. In Judges 5:7, during the crisis of judgment in Israel before Deborah, it signifies the absence of effective leaders — the failure of leadership in the face of Canaanite oppression. In Judges 5:11, it refers to the victorious leader, whose blessings deserve to be sung. These two uses show a notion of decision-making power and direction of the people, often absent or weak, sometimes restored by the hand of God.
H6520.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of godly and active leadership in service to God's people. When leaders are "lacking in strength," the people suffer; when God raises up a leader like Deborah, deliverance comes. This invites the reader to pray for authorities and to recognize that all true governing power comes from God for the protection and good of His people.

sens: Inhabited place without defensive walls
Rural area or dispersed habitat
By extension, inhabitant of these places
H6521.detail:
1. It is a locality without fortifications, exposed and without military protection. In Deuteronomy 3:5, the text distinguishes between "fortified cities, with high walls, gates, and bars" and "very numerous unwalled towns": this opposition shows that the word precisely designates the absence of these defenses.
2. It more broadly evokes an open, rural region, far from fortified centers. In Esther 9:19, the "Jews of the countryside, who live in unwalled towns" contrasts with walled cities: it is the outside world, accessible and vulnerable.
3. By extension, the word can also refer to the inhabitant of these uncovered spaces. In 1 Samuel 6:18, the "unwalled villages" of the Philistines are referred to as small, non-fortified centers, distinct from their major cities.
H6521.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of being "open, defenseless" or of a "cleared region." The word structurally contrasts with that which designates a fortified city: it is the quintessential vulnerable habitat, where the inhabitants live without architectural protection. The Hebrew language thus constructs a semantic pair: fortified/open, walled/unwalled.
H6521.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to describe a category of habitat. In Deuteronomy 3:5, Moses lists the conquests by distinguishing fortified cities from open cities. In 1 Samuel 6:18, the unwalled villages of the Philistines are counted. In Esther 9:19, it refers to rural and non-fortified Jewish communities. In all cases, the word carries an administrative and sociological dimension: it is a classification of human settlements according to their degree of protection.
H6521.portee: This word reminds us of the vulnerability of those who lack architectural or military protection. For God's people, it symbolizes a trust in divine protection rather than in walls: God guards Israel far better than any fortification. It is also a reflection of real life in the promised land, where most inhabitants live openly, without walls, in dependence on the providence of the Lord.

sens: people established in Canaan before the Israelite conquest
inhabitants of the rural and open areas of Canaan
H6522.detail:
1. The Pherezites are a people who lived in Canaan at the time Abraham arrived and before the Israelites conquered the land (Genesis 13:7). They are among the seven nations that God promises to drive out before Israel to give them the land in possession.
2. Their name suggests that they inhabited rather the villages and open areas, as opposed to other peoples established in fortified or mountainous cities. During the conquest led by Joshua, the Pherezites fought alongside other Canaanite peoples against Israel (Joshua 24:11).
H6522.origine: The name Pherezite likely comes from a Hebrew root evoking the village or the open, unfortified place. This is why it is understood that this people was established in the less densely built areas of Canaan, distinct from the inhabitants of large cities like Jericho or Jerusalem.
H6522.emploi: The Pherezites appear 23 times in the Bible, systematically mentioned alongside other Canaanite peoples: Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Hivites, and Jebusites. They are listed in God's promises to Abraham and Moses regarding the possession of Canaan (Genesis 13:7; Exodus 3:8), and then in the order of conquest given by God (Deuteronomy 20:17). During Joshua's conquest, they fight against Israel (Joshua 24:11 and Judges 1:4-5), but Israel gradually subdues them. After the conquest, they become forced laborers for the service of the temple and the palace (1 Kings 9:20).
H6522.portee: The Pherezites remind the reader that God promised Abraham a tangible land, promised to Israel in the divine plan, and occupied by peoples that God committed to drive out. Their repeated mention underscores the fulfillment of the promise made to the patriarchs and invites the reader to see God's trust in His people, even in the face of established and organized enemies.

sens: Dark gray metal, hard and resistant, which rusts in humid air
That which symbolizes strength, power, hardness
The rigor of an oppressive rule or regime
H6523.detail:
1. Iron is a dark gray metal, very hard and resistant, found in nature and can be worked. It is the material of tools, weapons, and chains. In Nebuchadnezzar's vision, the legs of the royal statue are made of iron (Daniel 2:33), symbolizing the solidity and duration of a kingdom.
2. Iron represents brute strength and invincibility. The statue has "something of the strength of iron" mixed with clay (Daniel 2:41): this indicates that a political power will retain some strength despite its internal weaknesses.
3. Iron also evokes oppressive rigor or constraint: the trunk of the cut tree is bound "with iron and bronze chains" (Daniel 4:15), an image of imprisonment and captivity imposed by a dominating sovereign.
H6523.origine: The Aramaic word parzel comes from the same root as the Hebrew barzel (H1270), attested since the earliest biblical texts. Iron was known and worked for a long time in the Near East: it was the metal of strength and royal domination. The term always designates the same precise, concrete, and indisputable material.
H6523.emploi: The word "iron" appears 14 times in the Aramaic Bible, exclusively in the book of Daniel (chapters 2, 4, 5, and 7). It is almost always used in prophetic visions: that of the statue with feet made of iron and clay (Daniel 2), that of the tree bound by iron chains (Daniel 4), and that of the iron beasts (Daniel 7). It is a term that carries a prophetic and symbolic dimension: it never designates the ordinary iron of tools or weapons of war, but iron as a manifestation of divine political power and the order of the world.
H6523.portee: Iron in Daniel's visions invites the reader to reflect on the power of human kingdoms. It reminds us that even what seems strong and durable—represented by this hard metal—cannot remain intact when the kingdom of God intervenes. For the believer, it is both a warning and a hope: no earthly power is eternal; only the kingdom founded by God will endure.

sens: To emit a shoot, a bud, to develop
To bloom, to give flowers
To prosper, to flourish (figurative sense)
To manifest, to grow (for an evil or a consequence)
H6524A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a plant that emits shoots and buds: the branches of the vine "push" and develop their flowers (Genesis 40:10). It is the image of new growth, of life resuming after dormancy: as it approaches water, the tree "pushes branches like a young plant" (Job 14:9).
2. The word more specifically designates blooming: the flowers that open, the plants that bloom. This is why the Segond often translates it as "to bloom" or "bloom." The arid desert will "be covered with flowers" (Isaiah 35:2).
3. Figuratively, it means to prosper or flourish: those who are planted in the house of God "prosper" in His courts (Psalms 92:14), meaning they develop and grow spiritually.
4. The word can also describe the growth of a negative consequence: punishment "germinates" like a poisonous plant in the furrows (Hosea 10:4), meaning it is born and develops.
H6524A.origine: The Hebrew root פרח expresses the idea of rapid and visible growth: a bud that bursts forth, a flower that blooms. The word is related to other Semitic roots denoting proliferation and multiplicity. In Hebrew, this family is found in words related to dispersion and flourishing. The image is always that of something unfolding and becoming visible.
H6524A.emploi: The verb appears 24 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in poems (Psalms, Song of Songs), the prophets (Isaiah, Hosea, Ezekiel), and narratives (Genesis, Job). It is used to describe the growth of plants (vines, trees, desert flowers) and easily extends to the figurative sense: the prosperity of a descendant (Proverbs 11:28), the manifestation of divine glory (Isaiah 66:14), or the emergence of judgment (Ezekiel 7:10). Its usage varies little from text to text: it is always the image of life that bursts forth and flourishes, naturally or symbolically.
H6524A.portee: This word invites the reader to see God as the one who makes grow and flourish. For the believer planted in the house of the Lord, "to push" becomes a promise of prosperity and life. It is also a reminder that God's blessing is not static, but alive, in constant growth—just like a plant that continues to push its branches and flowers.

sens: Sudden and visible appearance of a skin disease
Manifestation of an affliction that emerges or spreads on the surface of the body
H6524B.detail:
1. The word describes the appearance of a rash, particularly leprosy and pustules that arise on the skin. In Exodus 9:9, the plague of Egypt produces ulcers formed by an eruption of pustules on both men and animals. It is something that "comes out" of the skin, visible and manifest.

2. More broadly, the word designates any affliction that manifests or spreads on the body. In Leviticus 13:12, when leprosy erupts and covers the entire skin of the afflicted, the progression of the disease is recognized. The word emphasizes the moment when the disease becomes visible and spreads, not the disease itself but its appearance or development on the surface of the body.
H6524B.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּרַח (parach) literally means "to bloom," "to flourish," "to come out," or "to burst forth." It evokes the image of something that suddenly springs forth or emerges, like a flower opening or a phenomenon that suddenly appears. In biblical texts, it is used to describe anything that "bursts forth" or "appears" visibly and often suddenly, hence its application to skin symptoms that emerge and spread.
H6524B.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in Exodus 9 and Leviticus 13-14, in medical and ritual contexts. In Exodus 9, it describes the pustules of the fifth plague of Egypt that appear on men and animals. The remaining usages are found in the Levitical laws concerning leprosy: the priest must determine whether a skin affliction constitutes a true leprous plague declared unclean or a mere eruption without cultic consequence. The word thus marks the diagnostic moment when the disease becomes visible and when the priest must examine it to assess whether it renders the person unclean.
H6524B.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible takes physical illness and its visible manifestations seriously. The attention given to the details of these skin afflictions shows that God is also concerned about our bodily well-being. For the believer, recognizing and declaring one's illnesses, as the Israelites were to do before the priest, is to accept being known and to seek healing and purification from God.

sens: to take flight, leave the ground by flying
to escape, to free oneself from a hold
H6524C.detail:
1. To fly away describes the action of taking flight, lifting into the air, and moving away by flying — the concrete image of the upward movement of one who flies. In Ezekiel 13:20, the prophet speaks of souls that fly away, freed from the grip of false prophets: it is the movement of escape and liberation.
2. Figuratively, to fly away denotes escape, deliverance from a situation of oppression or capture — like prey escaping from the hands of its captor. It is this same verse that illustrates it: God snatches the souls from those who sought to trap them and makes them fly away to freedom.
H6524C.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּרַח (parach) comes from a root evoking flight and rapid movement. Although marked as an Aramaism in biblical Hebrew (influence from Aramaic, a sister language spoken during the exile), the word is rooted in the natural and universal image of a bird rising. The family of the word shares this idea of upward movement and flight.
H6524C.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 13:20. The prophet Ezekiel denounces the false prophetesses who, through magical cushions and occult practices, sought to "surprise" the souls — that is, to capture and enslave them. The Lord promises to intervene to deliver these souls so that they may fly away, meaning they are freed from this spiritual trap. The usage is unique but dense with meaning: it places flight in the service of divine deliverance.
H6524C.portee: This word reminds us that God's spiritual deliverance grants true freedom to those who accept it: not a selfish escape, but liberation from all spiritual domination. For the believer, the image of flight evokes regained lightness and escape from the traps of false doctrines and bad religious practices. It is an invitation to seek true freedom in God alone.

sens: Flower of a plant, bud or floral bloom
Ornament in the shape of a flower, decorative motif carved or sculpted
Blooming, prosperity, peak of something
H6525.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the flower itself, in a botanical sense: the bud or the fully opened flower of a plant. This is its simplest and most concrete usage. In passages about the lampstand (Exodus 25:31, Exodus 37:19), God requests that the stem of the lampstand be adorned with "flowers" of gold: these sculpted flowers imitate the natural shape of real flowers, serving as embellishments for the sacred light.
2. The word also designates a decorative motif, an ornament in the shape of a flower carved or molded from a material (gold, stone). For example, the edge of the large bronze basin of the temple was "shaped like a lily flower" (1 Kings 7:26), describing a sculpted decoration imitating the petals of a lily flower.
3. Rarely, the word takes on a more figurative meaning: the flower symbolizes blooming, freshness, brilliance — and sometimes their opposite, withering or an end. Isaiah 18:5 speaks of the flower that "withers," an image of ruin or an end.
4. By extension, a flower that blooms or dies evokes the ephemerality and vanity of what is beautiful but fragile.
H6525.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּרַח (perach) comes from a root that evokes the idea of "to bloom," "to bud," "to emerge." It is related to the image of the bud or flower that emerges and unfolds. The word is used both in the concrete sense (the flower itself) and in the sense of "floral decoration." In Hebrew, the lexical field of the plant and its growth is rich: the same word can describe both the natural bud and the ornamental motif that imitates it.
H6525.emploi: The word appears about fifteen times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in two contexts. First, it frequently appears in descriptions of the lampstand of the Tabernacle (Exodus 25:31, 25:33, 25:34; Exodus 37:17-20; Numbers 8:4): the "flowers" of gold are sculpted ornaments that adorn the stem and branches. Secondly, it appears in architectural descriptions of Solomon's temple, particularly for the large bronze basin (1 Kings 7:26; 2 Chronicles 4:5), where the edge is shaped in a floral motif. Finally, the word takes on a prophetic hue in the prophets (Isaiah 5:24, Isaiah 18:5; Nahum 1:4), where it evokes the blooming or withering of flowers as an image of prosperity or ruin.
H6525.portee: This word reminds us that God valued beauty and ornamentation in His place of worship. The lampstand and the basin of the temple, adorned with golden flowers, show that Israelite liturgy did not reject aesthetics but integrated it into worship. The flower, a biblical image of what is beautiful yet transient, also invites the believer to meditate on the ephemerality of earthly things and the stability of God alone.

sens: Miserable person, poor and despised
Weak or feeble creature
H6526.detail:
1. A person in a state of great misery, poverty, and social abandonment. Job uses this word to refer to the beggars and outcasts who rise against him: these "miserables" harass him, turn him against himself, reduce him to nothing. It is the image of those whom society has cast aside, reduced to extreme destitution.
2. More broadly, any weak, feeble, or contemptible creature — one that inspires pity or disdain. The Hebrew evokes a brute or a worthless being in the eyes of the world.
H6526.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of division or separation: the miserable one is in some way cut off from the rest of the community, rejected, fragmented. The Hebrew language thus builds its images on social rupture and isolation.
H6526.emploi: This name appears only once in the Bible, in Job 30:12. Job bitterly denounces those whom life has cast out — the poor, the degraded — who now take revenge on him now that he has fallen. The context shows Job confronted with the contempt of these little people whom he has probably once ignored or protected. It is a scene of total reversal: the one who was great and respected becomes the prey of the weak.
H6526.portee: This verse reminds the reader that every human being, no matter how marginalized or despised, possesses a dignity and power that can turn against those who oppress them. Job discovers that one cannot ignore the miserable of the earth with impunity. For the Christian, it is a lesson on the respect due to every person, including the most humiliated.

sens: Improvise without rigor, let one's voice wander without measure
H6527.detail: 1. To extravagate means to sing or play without control, allowing fantasy to take precedence over technique and order. In Amos 6:5, the wealthy of Israel "extravagate to the sound of the lute": they play music in a careless, improvised manner, lacking the mastery that characterized David, the great musician of the people. The word evokes a kind of musical babble, a melodic gibberish where one believes to show skill while merely rambling.
H6527.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּרַט (parat) expresses the idea of letting slip, of speaking without restraint. Its root suggests a certain dispersion or lack of coherence. The word is rare in the Old Testament; its exact meaning remains uncertain, but the context of Amos clearly indicates a critique of musical babble and clumsy improvisation.
H6527.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Amos 6:5. The prophet denounces the practices of wealthy Israelites who believe themselves refined musicians — like David — but who are merely extravagating to the sound of their instruments. It is a judgment on spiritual superficiality: these men lull themselves into illusions about their own excellence, while Amos confronts them with their true mediocrity and distance from the Davidic ideal.
H6527.portee: This word reminds believers of a spiritual danger: that of confusing religious agitation with true devotion. Like the wealthy of Israel who "extravagated" in music, one can think they are serving God zealously while producing only hollow noise. Amos calls us to clarity and humility: to serve God well is to imitate David not only in appearance but through authentic mastery, an attentive heart.

sens: The grapes that fall from the cluster during the harvest
The remnants of the grape intentionally left in the vineyard
H6528.detail:
1. This word refers to the grapes detached or fallen from the main cluster during harvesting. The image is that of an imperfect harvest where some grapes escape and scatter on the ground.
2. In the law given to Israel, this term applies to the remnants intentionally left in the vineyard: the owner was not to gather them but to leave them for the poor and the foreigner (Leviticus 19:10). It is an act of charity inscribed in the harvest itself.
H6528.origine: The Hebrew word פֶּרֶט comes from a root expressing the idea of rupture or separation: something that has detached or dispersed. The primary meaning is "what is broken, what falls." It is an uncommon word, specific to the agricultural vocabulary of the Bible.
H6528.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 19:10. It is found in the holiness code that regulates the life of the people of Israel. Associated with the rules of harvesting (such as the prohibition of completely gleaning the harvest or picking all the fruit from the tree), it emphasizes the moral obligation to provide for the needs of the most vulnerable by leaving a portion of the harvest available to them.
H6528.portee: This word reminds the believer that generosity towards the poor is not an optional choice but a requirement of divine justice. Even in the harvest, God wants the rich to remember the weak. It teaches that our goods are entrusted to us with the responsibility to share.

sens: The edible product that trees and plants yield
The harvest, what is gathered from the earth
Children, descendants, posterity
The result, the consequence of an action or a word
H6529.detail:
1. The fruit in the concrete sense: it is what a tree or plant produces, such as an apple or a grape. In Genesis 1:11, God commands the earth to produce "fruit trees yielding fruit according to their kind" — it is the food that plants create by themselves.
2. The harvest or what the earth provides: by extension, "fruit" refers to all the products of the earth that one enjoys. When the Hebrews taste the grapes of Canaan in Numbers 13:20, they bring back the "fruits of the land." This is also what Nehemiah 9:36 means: enjoying the "fruits and goods" of the soil.
3. Children or descendants: a powerful image — children are the "fruit" of the womb, the continuation of life. Psalms 127:3 expresses it clearly: "Children are a heritage from the Lord."
4. The result or consequence of an action: in a figurative sense, fruit becomes what one reaps from their deeds or words. Proverbs 12:14 says: "From the fruit of the mouth, one is filled with good things" — our words bear fruit. Proverbs 1:31 warns: the wicked eat "the fruit of their way" — the consequences of their choices.
H6529.origine: The Hebrew word פְּרִי comes from a root that means to produce, to bear, to grow. It is associated with natural fertility: everything that is produced, developed, multiplied. In Hebrew, this word is mainly used as a concrete noun (what the earth gives, what the body engenders), but also very often in a figurative sense, especially in Proverbs and Psalms, to speak of the effects or results of human conduct.
H6529.emploi: The word "fruit" appears 107 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is first found in the context of creation and agriculture: Genesis, Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and the historical books speak of the fruit of trees, fields, and the tithe taken from them. Gradually, the Bible uses it figuratively: the Psalms and especially Proverbs develop the image of fruit as a moral result — the fruit of wisdom, the fruit of justice, the fruit of the word — showing that every action, every word, bears its fruit, good or bad. Isaiah and Jeremiah also use it for descendants and messianic promises.
H6529.portee: This word reminds the Christian of a vital truth: our words, our actions, and our choices produce fruit, just as a tree bears fruit. By reading that "from the fruit of the mouth, one is filled with good things" (Proverbs 12:14), one understands that there is a spiritual harvest at every moment, that one reaps what they have sown. For the disciple of Jesus, the image invites examination of the fruit of their life: does it yield good fruit? It is also the image that Jesus takes up when he speaks of branches that must bear much fruit in John 15.

sens: One who uses brute force, who attacks without reason
One who steals, who plunders by force
One who kills, who sheds blood
Fierce, savage (referring to a beast)
Impulsive, brutal in behavior
H6530.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a man who resorts to physical violence, to brute force to impose his will or terrorize others. In Psalms 17:4, the psalmist guards himself "against the way of the violent," meaning against men who live by coercion and aggression.
2. It often qualifies the thief and the bandit who seizes the possessions of others by force. Jeremiah denounces the temple: "Is this house upon which my name is invoked a den of robbers?" (Jeremiah 7:11), referring to men who find refuge there after committing thefts and crimes.
3. The word applies to one who sheds blood, who kills mercilessly. Ezekiel 18:10 describes the violent son: "If he has a son who is violent, who sheds blood," bringing together the brutal nature and the murderous act.
4. It can also describe a wild and fierce beast. Isaiah 35:9 promises that "no fierce beast" will take the road of the redeemed, contrasting messianic safety with the threat of wild creatures.
5. Used adjectivally, the word expresses an impulsive and brutal temperament, as in Ezekiel 7:22 when "furious men enter" the sanctuary to profane it.
H6530.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of breaking, fracturing: the violent one is one who breaks order, who forces obstacles. The word belongs to a family that expresses rupture and breach. In biblical Hebrew, it is a dynamic creation: from the verb meaning "to shatter" arises the name of one who acts with this destructive brutality.
H6530.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in prophetic and wisdom texts (Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel). It designates sometimes a category of men (bandits, war criminals), sometimes a moral quality (the violent nature). In the prophets, it often takes on an eschatological dimension: the violent will be punished or excluded from the world to come (Isaiah 35:9). In Ezekiel and Daniel, it describes aggression against the people or the worship of God, highlighting the opposition between wild men and the divine plan.
H6530.portee: This word reminds the believer that violence in all its forms — theft, murder, brutality — is contrary to God's design and will be judged. It invites recognition that only the Lord can establish a world of justice where the violent have no place. For today's believer, it is a call not to follow the way of the violent, but to seek peace and justice.

sens: rigorous character, severity in treating a person
physical or moral violence exercised on someone
cruelty, lack of compassion
H6531.detail:
1. Hardness is the quality of one who treats someone without mercy, with a ruthless demand. The Egyptians reduced the Hebrews "to hard service" (Exodus 1:13), meaning they crushed them under the weight of merciless labor, leaving them no respite or humanity. It is a calculated, almost systematic severity.
2. Hardness can also be brutal violence and tyrannical oppression. When the shepherds dominated the sheep "with violence and with hardness" (Ezekiel 34:4), they mistreated them without reason, exhausting them instead of caring for them. The image of wounded, lost, or strayed sheep shows that hardness injures and destroys.
3. Hardness is the total absence of mercy and gentleness. The Law of Israel strictly forbids the master from dominating his slave "with hardness" (Leviticus 25:43 and 25:46): even in a power relationship, God demands compassion. It is the opposite of kindness.
H6531.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of tension, rigidity, that which does not bend. It is close to the image of a cord or a hand stretched out with force. Hardness is what refuses to yield, to soften, to take into account the weakness of others.
H6531.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the context of slavery or commandment. It first describes the cruelty of the Egyptians towards Israel in slavery (Exodus 1:13-14): it is the term that defines their oppressive regime. Then it reappears in the Law of Leviticus to prohibit this same hardness to Israelite masters towards their servants or brothers (Leviticus 25:43, 25:46, 25:53), showing that hardness is always a sin against divine order. Finally, Ezekiel accuses the shepherds (spiritual leaders) of Israel of having acted "with violence and with hardness" (Ezekiel 34:4) towards the flock. The word always describes an abuse of power: someone who has authority over another and abuses it mercilessly.
H6531.portee: Hardness is presented as the opposite of wisdom and the fear of God. The Law commands believers to reject hardness and to treat the weak with justice and gentleness, for God sees all. This word invites the reader to examine his own heart: in relationships where he has power (family, work, community), does he treat the other with compassion or with hardness? The biblical condemnation of hardness calls for tenderness and fairness.

sens: Thick and richly adorned curtain that separates two spaces in the tabernacle
Barrier that marks the impenetrable limit between ordinary man and the presence of God
Separation that conceals from view what cannot be seen without consequence
H6532.detail:
1. The veil is the great curtain of blue, purple, and scarlet, finely worked with cherubim, that divides the tabernacle into two parts (Exodus 26:31). It separates the holy place from the most holy place, where the ark of the covenant rests and where God manifests Himself. It is a piece of dense and magnificent fabric, not a simple transparent cloth.
2. This veil marks a sacred and terrifying limit: only the high priest can pass through it, and only once a year, on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2). Anyone who enters otherwise into the veil would die, for he would see God face to face, which man cannot endure. It is a barrier of protection as much as of separation.
3. The veil also conceals the mystery: it creates a zone of shadow and secrecy where God deigns to meet with His people through the high priest. It symbolizes that God is near but hidden, present but inaccessible to ordinary mortals.
H6532.origine: The Hebrew word probably comes from a root that evokes the idea of doubling or separation. It simply designates that which separates, that which acts as a screen. The veil of the tabernacle is the veil par excellence, the model that gives the word its full spiritual resonance in the Bible. No other object of worship is designated by this word with such symbolic weight.
H6532.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Exodus and Leviticus. It is encountered during the construction of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:31 and 36:35 describe its making) and in the instructions for the placement of the ark (Exodus 40:3). The priests regularly maintain it: the lamps burn before the veil (Exodus 27:21), the incense rises before the veil (Exodus 30:6). In the sacrifices for sin, the blood is sprinkled toward the veil, then before the veil (Leviticus 4:6, 4:17). The veil carries the presence of God, and crossing it remains the most serious act of worship.
H6532.portee: The veil teaches the believer that God, although present in the heart of the community, remains inaccessible to self-will and carnal desire. There is no relationship with God without mediation and without respect for the order He establishes. But the veil is also a promise: it shows that God wants to dwell among His people. The New Testament will reveal that this veil was the shadow of the reality in Christ: in Him, access to the Father is opened to all who believe.

sens: To rip or split a fabric, a garment, into pieces
To wear a torn garment as an outward sign of mourning or pain
H6533.detail:
1. To tear literally means to rip or split a fabric by mistreating it. The context of clothing is central: in Leviticus 10:6, Moses forbids Aaron from tearing his garments at the death of his sons, which was the natural reaction of mourning. In Leviticus 13:45, the leper wears torn garments as a mandatory mark of his state of ritual impurity.
2. The word takes on a cultural and religious value: tearing one's garments becomes the visible expression of inner distress, mourning, or guilt. It is an act that publicly manifests that one is in an extraordinary situation, either of loss or of rupture with normalcy. In Leviticus 21:10, the high priest, unlike ordinary priests, must never tear his garments, as his function requires intact dignity.
H6533.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּרַם (parar) is probably related to the idea of separating or tearing apart. The family of this word refers to actions of rupture, separation, or destruction. In the Bible, this verb is specifically used for fabrics and garments, rarely for other materials. It is a concrete and visible act, unlike many other terms that express mourning internally.
H6533.emploi: The verb to tear (parar) appears three times in the Bible, all in the Levitical code (Leviticus 10:6, 13:45, 21:10). It always refers to garments and always in a ritually significant context. In Leviticus 10:6, it is a prohibition: Aaron must restrain the natural gesture of mourning to remain a priest. In Leviticus 13:45, it is an obligation: the leper must wear torn garments to warn others. In Leviticus 21:10, it is again a prohibition for the high priest. The word invariably designates the action of tearing a fabric, always with a ritual or symbolic significance.
H6533.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, the body and garments are never insignificant: they express the inner state and the relationship with God. The prohibition for priests to tear their garments teaches that some called by God must maintain control over their emotional expression to remain worthy of their function. It is a lesson in personal sacrifice and prioritizing the service of God over immediate relief from pain.

sens: One of the ten sons of the wicked Haman
H6534.detail: Parmaschtha is one of the ten sons of Haman, the grand vizier who plotted to destroy all the Jews in the Persian empire. During the Jews' vengeance against their enemies, after Queen Esther thwarted the plot, Parmaschtha and his brothers were killed (Esther 9:9).
H6534.origine: The name means in Persian "the superior" or "one who surpasses." It is a proper name from the Persian period, attested only once in the Bible, reflecting the names of noble families in the empire.
H6534.emploi: Parmaschtha appears only once in the entire Bible, in Esther 9:9, in the list of the ten sons of Haman executed by the Jews. With his brothers, he represents the annihilation of the offspring of the one who sought to annihilate the Jewish people. This passage concludes the story of Esther's deliverance.

sens: A man from the time of the Exodus and the desert
Father of Elitsaphan, prince of the tribe of Zebulun
H6535.detail: Parnac is a character from the Old Testament known only by his mention in Numbers 34:25. He is the father of Elitsaphan, who was designated as prince of the tribe of Zebulun at the time when Israel was preparing to enter the promised land. His role was indirect: it was his son who was given the responsibility to participate in the division of Canaan among the twelve tribes.
H6535.origine: The name Parnac means "delicate" in Hebrew. Its etymology suggests an image of delicacy or fragility, although this does not reflect a particular characteristic reported in the biblical text. The name appears only once in Scripture.
H6535.emploi: Parnac is mentioned only once in Numbers 34:25, in the context where God commands Moses to designate ten princes to help divide the promised land among the tribes of Israel. Parnac is identified simply as the father of Elitsaphan, with no further details about his life or actions. He represents one of the patriarchal families of Israel during the time of the desert.

sens: To divide, share into two or more parts
To have split hooves or a split horn (for an animal)
To break, shatter
H6536.detail:
1. To split primarily means to divide something into two parts by separating it forcefully. It is the action of cutting or breaking to transform a unit into several pieces — for example, splitting wood in two.

2. When speaking of an animal, having a split horn or split hoof describes its physical conformation: a foot divided into two, as in cattle or goats. This physical trait determines whether the animal is clean or unclean according to the Law of Moses (Leviticus 11:3: "every animal that has split hooves").

3. To split can also mean to break, shatter something by separating it — an act of destruction or voluntary division.
H6536.origine: The Hebrew verb פָּרַס (paras) comes from a root that describes the action of dividing or separating into two. Its basic image is that of a clean separation: to split, divide, share. Aramaic uses the related word פְּרַס (peras) with the same meaning. The word is mainly used to describe the physical characteristics of animals — their split hooves — which mark their purity according to the Law.
H6536.emploi: This word appears 12 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the dietary purity codes of Leviticus and Deuteronomy. It specifically designates a trait of the animal: to have split hooves or a split horn (Leviticus 11:3-7; Deuteronomy 14:6-7). These passages enumerate the animals that Israel may eat: those that chew the cud AND have split hooves are clean. The Law uses this word to establish a clear distinction — a separation — between the clean and the unclean, showing how the verb "to split" also applies to the action of separating, dividing things into categories.
H6536.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the ancient Law taught Israel to discern, to "split" the clean from the unclean, not only in what they eat but in the heart. Although these dietary rules no longer bind the Christian, they reveal a lasting principle: God calls His people to moral distinction and holiness. Learning what was clean or unclean helped Israel cultivate obedience and recognize that life itself is sacred.

sens: Separate into parts, fragment
Distribute among several
Break the unity of something
H6537A.detail:
1. To divide means to cut, to separate something into two or more pieces. This is the concrete image of the word: breaking physical unity. In Daniel 5:28, the oracle announces that the kingdom of Belshazzar will be "divided" between the Medes and the Persians — it will not remain intact, but will be fragmented, with each of these powers receiving a share.
2. By extension, it means to distribute what was unique among several owners or rulers. The kingdom does not disappear, but its authority is shared.
3. In a figurative sense, it is to destroy the unity, integrity, or strength of something by breaking it apart. To divide a reign is to weaken it by fragmenting it.
H6537A.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew root פָּרַס (paras), which fundamentally means "to divide" or "to separate into two." The root evokes the idea of breaking or sharing.
